newsitem.title: UK: Narrow EMU still odds-on for 1999.
newsitem.headline: Narrow EMU still odds-on for 1999.

text.p: European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) remains odds-on to go ahead as scheduled on January 1, 1999, according to a Reuters monthly poll published on Monday.
The 41 European think-tanks and economists who took part in the survey predicted EMU stood on average an 82 percent chance of going ahead on time, unchanged from the October poll result.

"It's a political process that cannot be stopped now. It would take a change in the Maastricht Treaty and that's not feasible," said Professor Carlo Favero of Igier, of the research arm of Bocconi University in Milan.
EMU is expected to start with a membership of Austria, France, Germany, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, according to all of the poll contributors.
All but one said Belgium would also be a founder member -- Spain's Banco Bilbao Vizcaya said Belgium could miss out because of its failure to meet the budget deficit criterion.

"Belgium will find it difficult to be in the first wave because their deficit (as a ratio to general domestic product) will be greater than three percent," said Carmen Alcaide, director of macro-economic research at BBV in Madrid.
Although Belgium and Luxembourg already have a currency union, economists said there was a slim chance that Luxembourg could join EMU without Belgium.

Ireland and Finland had maintained a high probability of joining the core countries as founder members. Some 36 of the 41 respondents, or 88 percent, said Ireland would be likely to join in the first wave, compared to 33 out of 36 respondents (92 percent) in the October poll.

Some doubts over Ireland's entry still exist -- primarily because of its proximity to Britain, which has put the politically-sensitive EMU issue on the back-burner ahead of a national election due on or before May 1997.
Sterling's recent rally has put pressure on Irish inflation and prompted fears that interest rates may have to rise, and that could make it much harder for Ireland to qualify, experts said.
Jeremy Hawkins at Bank of America in London said that if the punt were to rise against the mark, it could give Germany the justification to keep Ireland ou.
"(But) if you rip sterling out of the equation, (the Irish) would definitely be in," he said.
Finland gains a high probability rating for being part of the currency union from the start, with 34 of the 41 respondents, or 83 percent, expecting to see Finland join the others in January 1999.

The poll showed that no more than 10 percent of respondents expected the southern fringe countries and Britain to join, although a number said Italy, Portugal and Spain's chances were steadily improving.
"In recent weeks the possiblity of Portugal, Spain and to a lesser extent Italy joining has increased," said Niels Thygesen, professor of economics at the University of Copenhagen.
"The continued convergence of interest rates in particular is a sign that the view of the financial markets has become steadily more positive on all three countries," he said.
